note.explanation: Alkanes are mostly unreactive, but your textbook describes two important reactions: halogenation and combustion. Halogenation replaces hydrogen atoms with halogen atoms in UV light. Combustion burns an alkane in oxygen to form carbon dioxide, water and heat.
note.checkAnswer: Combustion forms carbon dioxide and water, and releases heat.
note.simple: Alkanes do not react easily, but they can react with chlorine in UV light or burn in oxygen.
note.checkQuestion: What are the two important reactions of alkanes described in this section?
note.title: Important Reactions of Alkanes
steps: In halogenation, a halogen replaces a hydrogen atom in an alkane.
UV light is used, so this is called photochemical substitution.
In combustion, an alkane reacts with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O, releasing heat.
Methane reacts with chlorine to form chloromethane and hydrogen chloride.
note.answer: The two important reactions are halogenation (substitution) and combustion.

options: The carbon–hydrogen bonds are almost non-polar.
The carbon atoms have no shared electrons.
mcqs.stem: Why do alkanes show little chemical reactivity towards many laboratory reagents?
rationales: Correct: carbon and hydrogen share bonding electrons almost equally, making the bonds nearly non-polar.
Incorrect: carbon atoms do share electrons in their covalent bonds.
Incorrect: alkanes have covalent, not ionic, bonds.
Incorrect: alkanes contain carbon–hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.stem: What condition is used for the photochemical substitution of methane with chlorine?
rationales: Correct: the section shows chlorine substitution taking place in UV light.
Incorrect: water is not the stated condition for this reaction.
Incorrect: carbon dioxide is a combustion product, not a condition for halogenation.
Incorrect: hydrochloric acid is not the stated condition for halogenation.

options: The replacement of hydrogen in an alkane by a halogen atom
The addition of oxygen to form an alkene
The removal of carbon atoms from an alkane
The replacement of chlorine by hydrogen in water
mcqs.stem: Which description best defines substitution in alkane halogenation?
rationales: Correct: a hydrogen atom in the alkane is replaced by a halogen atom.
Incorrect: this does not describe the substitution reaction in the section.
Incorrect: removing carbon atoms is not the definition of substitution.
Incorrect: this is not the reaction described for alkane halogenation.

mcqs.stem: What are the products when methane reacts with chlorine in UV light in the first substitution step?
rationales: Correct: the section gives CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl in UV light.
Incorrect: the section shows HCl, not hydrogen gas, as a product.
Incorrect: methane is the reactant, and CH₃Cl is formed.
Incorrect: these are not the products of the first substitution step.

mcqs.stem: What does complete combustion of an alkane in oxygen produce, according to this section?
rationales: Correct: the section states that alkanes burn to form CO₂ and H₂O with heat released.
Incorrect: these are not the products given for complete combustion here.
Incorrect: chlorine is not produced by combustion of an alkane in oxygen.
Incorrect: methane and oxygen are reactants in this type of combustion.

options: Each further substitution can replace another hydrogen with chlorine.
The carbon atom changes into hydrogen.
Oxygen removes chlorine atoms from the product.
The reaction stops after one hydrogen is replaced.
mcqs.stem: What can happen when methane continues reacting with chlorine under UV light?
rationales: Correct: the section shows successive replacement leading to CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.
Incorrect: carbon does not change into hydrogen in this reaction.
Incorrect: oxygen is not involved in the successive chlorination shown.
Incorrect: the section shows that substitution can continue after the first hydrogen is replaced.

options: A large amount of heat is released.
The reaction absorbs all the heat from its surroundings.
mcqs.stem: Which energy change is associated with alkane combustion in this section?
rationales: Correct: the section says combustion evolves a large amount of heat.
Incorrect: the described combustion products are carbon dioxide and water, not an acid.
Incorrect: chlorine is not a combustion product in oxygen.
Incorrect: heat is released rather than absorbed according to the section.

options: Methane mixed with air can explode when ignited.
Methane is a liquid that cannot mix with air.
mcqs.stem: Why can leaked natural gas mixed with air be dangerous if ignited?
rationales: Correct: the section warns that natural gas (methane) and air may explode when ignited.
Incorrect: the section describes natural gas spreading and mixing with air, not as an immiscible liquid.
Incorrect: air does not turn methane into chlorine.
Incorrect: methane burns in oxygen and releases heat.

written.text: During the combustion reaction of ethane, which bonds are being broken and which are being formed?
written.finalAnswer: Broken: C—C, C—H and O=O bonds; formed: C=O and O—H bonds.

rubric.why: Identifies the bonds broken in the reactants.
rubric.how: List C—C, C—H and O=O bonds.

rubric.why: Identifies the bonds formed in the products.
rubric.how: List C=O and O—H bonds.

modelAnswer: Broken bonds: C—C, C—H and O=O.
Formed bonds: C=O and O—H.
Therefore, C—C, C—H and O=O bonds are broken, and C=O and O—H bonds are formed.

written.text: What products other than CH₃Cl are formed when methane reacts with chlorine gas?

rubric.why: Names the other product in the substitution equation.
rubric.how: Write HCl.

rubric.why: Gives the product's correct name as well as identifying it.
rubric.how: State hydrogen chloride.

modelAnswer: CH₄ + Cl₂  hν→ CH₃—Cl + H—Cl
The other product is H—Cl, hydrogen chloride.

written.text: Why do alkanes show little reactivity towards the other reagents?
written.finalAnswer: Alkanes are almost non-polar because the bonding electrons in C—H and C—C bonds are almost equally shared. Reagents such as acids, bases and oxidizing agents have no reaction site to attach to.

rubric.why: States the key property used to explain low reactivity.
rubric.description: State that alkanes are almost non-polar.
rubric.how: Connect the explanation to the non-polar nature of alkanes.

rubric.why: Identifies the bonds whose electrons are shared almost equally.
rubric.description: Refer to the C—H and C—C bonds.
rubric.how: Name both bond types.

rubric.why: Explains why the bonds are nearly non-polar.
rubric.description: Explain how the bonding electrons are shared.
rubric.how: Say that the electrons are almost equally shared.

rubric.why: Completes the link to the behaviour of reagents.
rubric.description: Explain why many reagents do not react.
rubric.how: State that reagents have no reaction site to which they can attach.

modelAnswer: The electronegativity values of carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.1) do not differ appreciably.
The bonding electrons in C—H and C—C bonds are almost equally shared, making alkanes almost non-polar.
Acids, bases and oxidizing agents find no reaction site in alkane molecules to which they could be attached.
Therefore, alkanes show little reactivity towards these reagents.

written.text: Why does a mixture of natural gas and air explode?
written.finalAnswer: Natural gas (methane) mixed with air may explode when ignited because it burns rapidly and releases a large amount of heat.

rubric.why: Identifies the combustible mixture involved.
rubric.description: Identify the components of the mixture.
rubric.how: State that natural gas (methane) mixes with air.

rubric.why: Names the condition that can trigger the explosion.
rubric.how: Mention ignition.

rubric.why: Connects ignition to the chemical reaction.
rubric.how: State that the gas mixture burns.

rubric.why: Includes the energy release associated with the reaction.
rubric.how: State that a large amount of heat is released.

modelAnswer: Natural gas is methane, and it can mix with air.
When the mixture is ignited, it burns rapidly.
Combustion releases a large amount of heat.
Therefore, the natural gas–air mixture may explode when ignited.

written.text: Reactions of alkanes with chlorine takes place in the presence of sunlight. What is the role of sunlight in the reaction?
written.finalAnswer: Sunlight, especially UV light, provides the condition for the photochemical substitution reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies the type of light specified for the reaction.
rubric.how: State UV or ultraviolet light.

rubric.why: Uses the correct name for the reaction carried out in light.
rubric.how: Call it photochemical substitution.

rubric.why: Identifies what the light-supported reaction does.
rubric.how: Mention substitution of hydrogen by chlorine.

rubric.why: Explains the role of sunlight in the stated method.
rubric.how: Say that the reaction takes place in the presence of UV light.

modelAnswer: Alkanes react with chlorine in the presence of UV light.
In this reaction, hydrogen is replaced by chlorine.
Since the substitution reaction is carried out in UV light, it is called a photochemical substitution reaction.

written.text: How combustion reaction of alkanes is useful for us?
written.finalAnswer: Combustion of alkanes releases a large amount of heat, which is useful as a source of energy, for example for cooking and heating.

rubric.why: Identifies the reaction being discussed.
rubric.how: Refer to combustion or burning of alkanes.

rubric.why: Identifies what the alkane burns in.
rubric.description: State the reactant needed for burning.
rubric.how: Mention oxygen or air.

rubric.why: Shows the main products of complete combustion.
rubric.how: State that carbon dioxide and water are formed.

rubric.why: Identifies the useful energy output.
rubric.how: Mention that a large amount of heat is released.

rubric.why: Links the released heat to a practical use.
rubric.description: Give a use of the released heat.
rubric.how: Give cooking, heating or another suitable energy use.

modelAnswer: Alkanes burn in oxygen or air to form CO₂ and H₂O.
This combustion reaction evolves a large amount of heat.
The released heat can be used as a source of energy, such as for cooking and heating.
Thus, combustion of alkanes is useful because it provides heat and energy.

written.text: When natural gas valve is kept open in the kitchen, the gas spreads through the whole kitchen. This may cause an explosion. What is the reason of this explosion and how can you avoid it?
written.finalAnswer: Leaked natural gas mixes with air and may explode if ignited. Close the valve, avoid flames and sparks, and ventilate the area safely.

rubric.why: Identifies the mixture that can become explosive.
rubric.how: State that natural gas mixes with air.

rubric.why: Identifies how the mixture can be set off.
rubric.how: Mention ignition, a spark or a flame.

rubric.why: States the danger that must be prevented.
rubric.how: Say the mixture may explode.

rubric.why: Gives the immediate step to stop more gas entering the kitchen.
rubric.how: Close the gas valve.

rubric.why: Gives a further sensible step to reduce danger.
rubric.how: Ventilate safely and keep away from flames or sparks.

modelAnswer: Natural gas may spread through the kitchen and mix with air.
The gas–air mixture may explode if it is ignited.
Close the gas valve and do not use flames or create sparks.
Ventilate the area safely and get help if needed.

For a halogenation equation, show UV light (hν) over the arrow and include HCl as a product when methane reacts with chlorine.
In a combustion question, write the products CO₂ and H₂O and show that heat is released; balance the equation if asked.
For bond questions, distinguish bonds broken in the reactants from bonds formed in the products.
For explanation marks, write the cause-and-effect link: nearly non-polar bonds mean reagents have no suitable reaction site.

The products contain C=O bonds in carbon dioxide and O—H bonds in water.

example.question: Write the combustion reaction of methane shown in this section.

explain.title: Alkanes are mostly unreactive
explain.body: Carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativity values. The electrons in C—H and C—C bonds are almost equally shared, so alkanes are almost non-polar. Many reagents therefore find no reaction site to attach to.

explain.title: Halogenation is substitution
explain.body: In a substitution reaction, a hydrogen atom in an alkane is replaced by a halogen atom. Chlorine reacts with alkanes in UV light, so this is called photochemical substitution. Methane first forms chloromethane and hydrogen chloride; further substitution can replace more hydrogen atoms.

explain.title: Combustion releases heat
explain.body: Alkanes burn in oxygen or air. Complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water, with a large amount of heat released.

mistakes: Do not call halogenation an addition reaction: the section defines it as substitution.
Do not omit HCl from the methane-and-chlorine equation.
Do not forget to show UV light (hν) for the photochemical substitution reaction.
Do not write only CO₂ for combustion; water is also formed.
Do not say the bonds in alkanes are ionic; they are nearly non-polar covalent bonds.
Keep bonds broken separate from bonds formed when explaining ethane combustion.
